finding.claim: The user identity is read directly from the client-supplied request header X-Session-User-Verified. Nothing in the code authenticates it, for example with a signature, session lookup or proxy-only trust. Any caller can set the header to the name of a user who holds grants and so gain that user's delete and write permissions. This is an authentication bypass that defeats the ACL.
finding.source: The attacker-controlled HTTP request header X-Session-User-Verified. The attacker only needs to know or guess a grantee's identifier, which is the key in resource['grants'].
finding.sink: DELETE /files/<fid> at views.py:14-19 (ensure_allowed then del STORE[fid]) and POST /files/<fid>/rename at views.py:22-28 (is_allowed then f['name'] = ...). Both authorize on g.user.

trace.note: before_request sets g.user = request.headers.get('X-Session-User-Verified') with no validation.
is_allowed checks only whether the action is in resource['grants'][user], so a spoofed name passes.
The file is deleted from STORE.
rename_file uses the same g.user check, then the file name is overwritten at views.py:27.

finding.guards_checked: I found no signature or HMAC check on the header, no session or token validation, and no middleware that strips the header from external requests. The repo contains only views.py and acl.py, so no reverse proxy or gateway config is visible. The header name suggests an upstream proxy sets it, but the app does not enforce that. If a trusted proxy overwrites the header and the app is not directly reachable, the risk drops. Nothing in the repo shows this. Requests with no header give user None, and grants.get(None) does not match a normal grantee, so only a supplied header is exploitable. The ACL check itself in acl.py is logically correct.

verdict.guard_found: none in repo; ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10) aborts 403 and is_allowed (views.py:25) is tested, but both only authorize the header-derived user
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate (views.py:11 trusts the header unvalidated, acl.py:5 matches the grants, views.py:17-18 and 25-27 act on the result), but the header name "X-Session-User-Verified" implies an upstream proxy sets and overwrites it, so exploitability depends on deployment, which the repo (views.py, acl.py only) doesn't show.
